query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine-learning model that integrates high-fidelity simulation data (from molecular dynamics and density functional theory capturing defect and impurity scattering) with experimental conductivity measurements can predict the electrical (and thermal) transport properties of HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than traditional analytical models based on perfect, defect‐free crystals. The model will achieve improved predictions in both the low-temperature (0–200 K, where quantum scattering dominates) and high-temperature (300–1200 K, where phonon and defect scattering are significant) regimes, including for samples with 1 wt.% oxygen.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy, considered in two states – an ideal, defect‐free crystal and a specimen with 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Application of a machine-learning framework (e.g., neural network or graph neural network) trained on simulation outputs that explicitly include parameters for defect and oxygen impurity scattering, together with available experimental conductivity data.
generation.conditions: Temperature regimes split into (i) 0–200 K (low-temperature, where quantum scattering and potential localization effects are important) and (ii) 300–1200 K (high-temperature, where phonon scattering and defect interactions, including those induced by a 1 wt.% oxygen content, are significant).
generation.structural_mediator: Incorporation of descriptors representing defect density, oxygen impurity distribution, and related scattering parameters obtained from detailed simulations, which mediate the relationship between the alloy’s microstructure and its transport properties.
generation.mechanism: The machine-learning approach learns non-linear correlations between temperature, defect/impurity features, and transport behavior. By ‘seeing’ realistic scattering mechanisms in the training data, it can interpolate and predict conductivity more accurately than analytical models that assume a perfect lattice.
generation.predicted_outcome: Model predictions for conductivity in both pristine and oxygen-doped specimens will be within ±5% of experimental measurements, outperforming traditional analytical predictions that typically deviate by margins larger than ±15%.
generation.baseline: Traditional analytical models that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals and do not account for impurity scattering, which have known accuracy limitations over the specified temperature ranges.
generation.boundary: The improved predictive accuracy is expected to hold for temperatures between nearly 0 K and 1200 K and for samples with up to 1 wt.% oxygen. Outside these ranges (e.g., presence of higher impurity levels or extreme cryogenic/ultrahigh-temperature conditions), the model’s accuracy may degrade.
generation.uncertainty: While the integrated machine-learning approach is expected to capture complex scattering mechanisms more accurately, the exact magnitude of improvement may depend on the quality and breadth of the simulation and experimental data used for training. Additionally, potential unmodeled mechanisms or rare defect types could introduce prediction errors.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one pristine and one doped with 1 wt.% oxygen. Measure electrical conductivity at selected temperatures across the two regimes (e.g., 150 K and 800 K) under controlled conditions. Compare the measured conductivities with the predictions made by the machine-learning model.
measurements: Electrical conductivity at ~150 K for the pristine specimen
Electrical conductivity at ~800 K for the oxygen-doped specimen
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the machine-learning model’s predictions differ from the experimentally measured conductivity by more than ±5% in either temperature regime, then the hypothesis that the approach significantly improves predictive accuracy over traditional analytical models is falsified.

Data Availability Statement

The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.

Because modern jet engines require larger and larger parameters, improved creep properties are essential for the aerospace industry. The currently used Ni-based superalloys are reaching their limits, and since the beginning of the 21st century new alloys known as High Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have begun to look attractive [ [1] , [2] ]. HEAs can be regarded as solid solution alloys that contain at least five alloying elements in equal or near equal atomic percentages, and this large number of alloying elements results in maximizing the configurational entropy of the disordered solid solution. However, the microstructure of certain HEAs can include nano-precipitates, ordered solid-solution phases, disordered solid-solution phases, and even amorphous phases [ [1] , [2] ]. frame.system: Bulk high‐entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr prepared in two forms: (a) an idealized, defect‐free crystal and (b) a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen as a controlled impurity.
frame.goal: To predict transport properties (e.g., electrical and/or thermal conductivity) accurately across a wide temperature range (from nearly 0 K up to 1200 K) by developing a predictive approach that explicitly incorporates the effects of defects and impurities.
frame.limitation: Existing analytical predictions are limited by their reliance on perfect, defect‐free crystal models, which fail to capture disorder-induced scattering mechanisms and the impact of oxygen impurities, leading to inaccurate conductivity predictions in both low-temperature (0–200 K) and high-temperature (300–1200 K) regimes.

decision.trend: Earlier studies on high‐entropy alloys, including Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (PMC5578249) and HfNbTaTiZr prepared via additive manufacturing (PMC11077685), have primarily focused on predicting mechanical properties and phase behavior using models that assume ideal, nearly defect‐free crystals. Although these works have meticulously characterized the impact of casting, processing, and even controlled impurity content (e.g., ~1 wt.% oxygen in PMC11077685) on strength, hardness, and microstructural evolution, none have successfully extended such predictive capabilities to transport properties like electrical or thermal conductivity. In particular, the persistent reliance on perfect-lattice approximations has left the accurate prediction of conductivity over the wide temperature range (0–200 K with potential quantum effects and 300–1200 K with phonon and defect scattering) unresolved.
decision.unsolved: No current predictive methodology explicitly accounts for the scattering mechanisms induced by real-life defects and oxygen impurities in HfNbTaTiZr, leading to inaccuracies in modelling transport properties, especially given the non-linear temperature dependence across low and high regimes.
decision.lever: Develop a machine-learning model (e.g., a neural network or graph neural network) that integrates high-fidelity simulation outputs (from MD and density functional theory capturing defect/impurity scattering parameters) with experimental conductivity data. Key parameters would include temperature as a continuous variable and descriptors for defect concentration and oxygen content.
decision.why: Machine-learning approaches can capture the complex, non-linear interactions arising from disorder and impurity scattering that traditional analytical models miss. Building on the trend of incorporating realistic microstructural features—as evidenced by the experimental differences between pristine and oxygen-doped specimens in PMC11077685—this method promises improved accuracy over defect‐free predictions while delineating clear temperature and sample applicability limits. A held-out benchmark, for example a measured electrical conductivity at 150 K or 800 K that the model must predict within a ±5% error margin, can serve as a falsification criterion if deviations exceed this threshold.
